title: Corporations Act 2001 (Cth), Chapter 7 (Financial services and markets), selected provisions

verification_notes: Checked against the authorised compilation on the Federal Register of Legislation: Compilation No. 149, compilation date 19 September 2026 (C2026C00432), volumes 4 and 5. Confirmed section text for 765A(1)(c), 766G, 912A (including civil penalty in 912A(5A)), 912D, 912DAA (30 day deadline is in s912DAA(3); civil penalty in s912DAA(7)), 941A, 949A, 961B, 992A, 994B, 994C, 994E, 994F (10 business day clocks in s994F(4), (5) and (6)), 994G and 1041H. Statutory s912D(1)(c) investigation threshold is 30 days; ASIC Corporations and Credit (Breach Reporting: Reportable Situations) Instrument 2024/620 s6A modifies this to 60 days (per RG 78 as updated August 2025); the instrument itself was not opened. Commencement dates for the 2021 reforms (breach reporting 1 October 2021; DDO and the new hawking prohibition 5 October 2021; claims handling as a financial service 1 January 2021 with transition to 1 January 2022) come from ASIC guidance (RG 78, RG 274, RG 38, REP 768), not from the endnotes. Health insurance provided as part of a health insurance business, and health-related business through a health benefits fund, are not financial products under s765A(1)(c) and (ca), so these Chapter 7 provisions do not apply to private health insurance products; they can apply to a private health insurer that distributes general or life insurance (for example travel or pet cover) under an AFS licence or as an authorised representative.

summary: Chapter 7 of the Corporations Act regulates financial products and services, including general and life insurance. Key provisions for insurers and their distributors are the AFS licensee general obligations (efficiently, honestly and fairly; IDR; resources; risk management), the claims handling and settling financial service, mandatory self-reporting of reportable situations to ASIC within 30 days, Financial Services Guide and general advice warning obligations, the best interests duty for personal advice, the hawking prohibition, the design and distribution obligations (target market determinations, reasonable steps, and 10 business day reporting clocks), and the civil prohibition on misleading or deceptive conduct. Private health insurance products are not financial products for Chapter 7.

clauses.section_name: Part 7.1 Division 4: Meaning of financial service and related terms
clauses.heading: Meaning of claims handling and settling service
clauses.text: A person provides a claims handling and settling service if, in response to an inquiry about an existing or potential claim under an insurance product, they make a recommendation or state an opinion that could reasonably influence whether to make or continue the claim, or if they assist a person to make a claim, represent an insured in pursuing a claim, assess or help assess insurer liability, decide to accept or reject all or part of a claim, quantify or help quantify the insurer's liability, offer to settle, or satisfy the insurer's liability in settlement. The service is treated as provided to the insured, including a third party beneficiary.
subclauses: (1)(a) Recommendations or opinions about an existing or potential claim that could influence the claim decision.
(1)(b) to (c) Assisting with or representing an insured in a claim.
(1)(d) to (f) Assessing liability, deciding to accept or reject, and quantifying liability.
(1)(g) to (h) Offering to settle and satisfying liability in settlement.
(2) Service treated as provided to the insured or third party beneficiary.
clauses.notes: An AI agent that triages, assesses, decides, quantifies or offers settlement on claims is providing a regulated financial service on the insurer's licence, so s912A (efficiently, honestly and fairly), breach reporting and RG 271 IDR apply to its conduct. Regime commenced 1 January 2021 with insurers required to comply from 1 January 2022 (ASIC REP 768). Some activities by repairers and certain service providers are carved out by regulation and s912A(1)(ca). Not applicable to private health insurance claims.

clauses.section_name: Part 7.6 Division 3: Obligations of financial services licensees
clauses.heading: General obligations
clauses.text: An AFS licensee must do all things necessary to provide its financial services efficiently, honestly and fairly; manage conflicts of interest; comply with licence conditions and financial services laws; take reasonable steps to ensure representatives comply; comply with the reference checking protocol; have adequate financial, technological and human resources (subject to an exception for APRA-regulated bodies); maintain competence; ensure representatives are trained and competent; for retail clients, have an IDR procedure meeting ASIC standards plus AFCA membership and give ASIC IDR data; have adequate risk management systems (APRA-regulated bodies excepted); and meet prescribed obligations.
subclauses: (1)(a) Efficiently, honestly and fairly.
(1)(aa) Adequate conflicts of interest arrangements.
(1)(b) to (ca) Comply with licence conditions and financial services laws, and take reasonable steps for representative compliance (with a claims-service carve-out for certain suppliers).
(1)(cc) Reference Checking and Information Sharing Protocol.
(1)(d) to (f) Adequate resources including technological resources; competence; trained and competent representatives.

(1)(g) Dispute resolution system for retail clients (IDR complying with ASIC standards, which includes enforceable parts of RG 271 via ASIC Instrument 2020/98, and AFCA membership) and IDR data reporting to ASIC.
(1)(h) Adequate risk management systems.
(5A) Civil penalty for contravening (1)(a), (aa), (ca), (cc), (d), (e), (f), (g), (h) or (j).
clauses.notes: The overarching standard for AI agent conduct on an insurer's licence. Deploying an AI agent must not degrade service quality; the licensee needs adequate technological resources, monitoring and competence to supervise it. Civil penalty applies to most limbs (s912A(5A)). These are core obligations, so significant breaches are reportable within 30 days under s912DAA. Not applicable to private health insurance products.

clauses.section_name: Part 7.6 Division 3: Obligations of financial services licensees
clauses.heading: Meaning of reportable situation
clauses.text: A reportable situation arises where the licensee or a representative has significantly breached a core obligation, is no longer able to comply with a core obligation and the breach would be significant, has investigated whether such a breach exists for more than the threshold period, or concludes such an investigation finding no reportable breach. Gross negligence in providing a financial service, serious fraud, and prescribed circumstances are also reportable. Core obligations include s912A and 912B duties and specified financial services laws, including for insurers the Insurance Contracts Act. A breach is deemed significant if it is a serious offence, a civil penalty contravention (unless excluded), a breach of the misleading or deceptive conduct provisions (s1041H(1) or ASIC Act s12DA(1)), or causes or is likely to cause material loss or damage to clients; otherwise significance is assessed against listed factors.
subclauses: (1)(a) to (b) Significant breach or likely significant breach of a core obligation.

(1)(c) to (d) Investigation into a possible significant breach that continues beyond the threshold (30 days in the Act, modified to 60 days by ASIC Instrument 2024/620 s6A), and the outcome of such an investigation if no breach is found.
(2) Gross negligence, serious fraud, and prescribed circumstances.

(3) Core obligations, including s912A, s912B, Chapter 7, ASIC Act Div 2, and APRA-administered laws prescribed by reg 7.6.02A (including the Insurance Act 1973, Insurance Contracts Act 1984 and Life Insurance Act 1995).
(4) Deemed significant breaches.
(5) Factors for assessing significance otherwise.
clauses.notes: Any AI agent incident (for example systematic misstatement of cover, wrongful claim declines, or failure to give IDR responses) must be routed into the licensee's incident and breach register and assessed against s912D. Misleading statements by an agent are deemed significant. Regime commenced 1 October 2021. Not applicable to private health insurance products.

clauses.section_name: Part 7.6 Division 3: Obligations of financial services licensees
clauses.heading: Obligation to lodge a report: reportable situations in relation to the financial services licensee
clauses.text: If there are reasonable grounds to believe a reportable situation has arisen, the licensee must lodge a report with ASIC in the prescribed form within 30 days after it first knows, or is reckless as to whether, there are reasonable grounds to believe the situation has arisen. An APRA-regulated licensee is taken to have lodged if it gave APRA a report containing all the required information, and is excused where its auditor or actuary reports the matter to APRA before or within 10 business days after the licensee first knows. Failure is a strict liability offence and a civil penalty contravention.
subclauses: (1) Must lodge a report with ASIC where there are reasonable grounds to believe a reportable situation has arisen.
(2) Prescribed form, in writing (lodged through the ASIC Regulatory Portal).
(3) Deadline: within 30 days after the licensee first knows, or is reckless as to whether, there are reasonable grounds to believe the situation has arisen.
(4) Strict liability.
(5) Report given to APRA with all required information is treated as lodged with ASIC.
(6) Exception where the auditor or actuary reports to APRA before, or within 10 business days after, the licensee first knows.
(7) Civil penalty provision.
(8) Knowledge and recklessness have their Criminal Code meanings.
clauses.notes: The 30 day clock is in s912DAA(3). Monitoring of AI agents should be designed so that reportable situations are detected and escalated quickly enough to investigate and lodge within 30 days. ASIC Instrument 2024/620 s7 allows a further related reportable situation to be reported within 90 days in limited cases (RG 78.84). Commenced 1 October 2021. Not applicable to private health insurance products.

clauses.heading: Obligation on financial services licensee to give a Financial Services Guide if financial service provided to person as a retail client
clauses.text: A licensee that provides a financial service to a retail client must give the client a Financial Services Guide in accordance with Division 2, subject to the exceptions in s941C. Failure is a civil penalty contravention.
subclauses: (1) Must give an FSG when providing a financial service to a retail client.
(2) Subject to s941C exceptions (for example where the client already has the information, or for some product issuers dealing in their own products).
(3) Civil penalty provision.
clauses.notes: An AI agent acting as a distribution channel (especially for brokers or authorised representatives) must ensure the FSG is provided at the right time, or that an exception applies. Timing rules are in s941D (not reproduced). Section 941B imposes the parallel duty on authorised representatives. Not applicable to private health insurance products.

clauses.heading: General advice provided to retail client: obligation to warn client that advice does not take account of client's objectives, financial situation or needs
clauses.text: When a licensee or authorised representative gives general advice to a retail client, it must warn the client that the advice does not take account of their objectives, financial situation or needs, that they should consider its appropriateness, and, where the advice relates to acquiring a particular product, that they should obtain and consider the PDS. The warning must be given at the same time and by the same means as the advice. Licensees must take reasonable steps to ensure authorised representatives comply.
subclauses: (1) Applies to general advice to retail clients by a licensee or authorised representative, unless regulations exempt.
(2) Required warning content, including the PDS recommendation where a particular product is involved.
(3) Same time and same means as the advice.
(4) Defence for representatives who followed reasonable licensee instructions.
(5) Licensee must take reasonable steps to ensure authorised representatives comply.
clauses.notes: Core runtime control for conversational agents: whenever the agent's output amounts to general advice (for example describing why a product suits people like the customer), it must give the warning in the same channel at the same time. Failure is an offence (s1311). If the agent considers the customer's personal circumstances it may be giving personal advice, triggering s961B. Not applicable to private health insurance products.

clauses.heading: Provider must act in the best interests of the client
clauses.text: A person giving personal advice to a retail client must act in the client's best interests. The duty is satisfied if the provider proves it identified the client's disclosed objectives, situation and needs and the subject matter of the advice, made reasonable inquiries where information was incomplete or inaccurate, assessed whether it had the expertise to advise (declining if not), where relevant investigated and assessed suitable products, based judgements on the client's relevant circumstances, and took any other step reasonably in the client's best interests. For advice on general insurance products, the duty is satisfied by taking only the first three steps.
subclauses: (1) Duty to act in the client's best interests.
(2)(a) to (g) Safe harbour steps.
(3) Reduced steps for ADI staff advising on basic banking, general insurance or consumer credit insurance.
(4) For general insurance products, the duty is satisfied by the steps in (2)(a), (b) and (c).
clauses.notes: Civil penalty via s961K for licensees. An AI agent that tailors recommendations to the customer's circumstances is giving personal advice and must satisfy this duty (fully for life insurance; the reduced steps for general insurance), and the agent must recognise when to decline. Most insurers design agents to stay within factual information or general advice. Not applicable to private health insurance products.

clauses.heading: Prohibition on hawking of financial products
clauses.text: A person must not offer a financial product to a retail client, or request or invite them to apply for or buy one, in the course of or because of an unsolicited contact. Unsolicited contact means a telephone call, face-to-face meeting or other real-time interaction in the nature of a conversation, where the consumer did not consent, or the consent fails the statutory requirements: the consent must be given before the contact, be positive and voluntary, be clear, cover the product (or the product must be reasonably within its scope), be followed in any form of contact specified, be given within 6 weeks before contact (or up to 12 weeks if a medical examination is needed), and not have been withdrawn. Exceptions apply for personal advice under the best interests duty, certain add-on insurance offers within the deferred sales model framework, and prescribed offers.
subclauses: (1) General prohibition for retail clients.
(2) Exceptions: personal advice subject to the best interests duty; add-on insurance linked to a principal product (limited by (3)); prescribed offers.
(4) Unsolicited contact: real-time contact without valid consent.
(5)(a) to (h) Consent requirements, including 6 week validity (12 weeks for medical examination).
(6) Consent may be varied or withdrawn at any time in any form.
(7) Advertising compliant with ss734 and 1018A is not unsolicited contact.
(9) Strict liability offence.
Related s992AA: consumer right of return and full refund.
clauses.notes: Directly constrains outbound or proactive AI agents (voice bots, live chat, messaging that is real-time and conversational). The agent must verify a valid, in-scope, unexpired consent before making any offer, and must not elicit consent during an unsolicited contact. Breach is a strict liability offence (RG 38 states maximums of 60 penalty units or 6 months imprisonment for individuals and 600 penalty units for bodies corporate) and gives a right of return. The current prohibition commenced 5 October 2021. Not applicable to private health insurance products.

clauses.section_name: Part 7.8A Division 2: Target market determinations for financial products
clauses.heading: Target market determinations for financial products
clauses.text: An issuer of a product requiring a PDS (including general and life insurance) must make a written target market determination before any person engages in retail product distribution conduct. The TMD must describe the target market, distribution conditions, review triggers, maximum review periods, complaints reporting periods for distributors, and other information distributors must report. It must be appropriate: distribution under the conditions should make it likely that retail clients are in the target market, and the product should likely be consistent with their likely objectives, financial situation and needs. The TMD must be publicly available free of charge.
subclauses: (1) to (2) Must make a TMD before distribution.
(3) Excluded products (for example MySuper, margin lending, most ordinary shares, and prescribed products such as medical indemnity insurance).
(5) Content requirements, including review triggers and complaints reporting periods.
(8) Appropriateness requirements.
(9) TMD must be publicly available free of charge.
Offence and civil penalty for key subsections.
clauses.notes: An AI sales or quote agent must have access to the current TMD and distribution conditions for each product and apply them in eligibility checks. DDO commenced 5 October 2021. Not applicable to private health insurance products (not financial products).

clauses.section_name: Part 7.8A Division 2: Target market determinations for financial products
clauses.heading: Target market determinations to be reviewed
clauses.text: An issuer must complete a review of its TMD within each review period while the product is on offer. If it knows that a review trigger, or an event reasonably suggesting the TMD is no longer appropriate, has occurred, it must stop distribution conduct from as soon as practicable, and no later than 10 business days after first knowing, unless it has reviewed the TMD and either made a new one or confirmed it remains appropriate. Distributors that know of the issuer's notice must likewise stop distributing.
subclauses: (1) Issuer may review or remake a TMD at any time.
(2) Must complete a review within each review period.
(3) Issuer must stop distribution conduct from as soon as practicable, and no later than 10 business days, after first knowing of a review trigger or similar event, unless it has reviewed the TMD.
Remaining subsections: related stop-distribution obligations on issuers and on regulated persons who know the TMD may no longer be appropriate.
clauses.notes: Agent complaint and outcome data (for example rising declines, cancellations or complaints) may be a review trigger. Distribution through an AI channel must be capable of being switched off within 10 business days. Offence and civil penalty.

clauses.section_name: Part 7.8A Division 3: Distribution of financial products
clauses.heading: Reasonable steps to ensure consistency with target market determinations
clauses.text: Issuers must take reasonable steps that will, or are reasonably likely to, result in retail distribution (other than excluded conduct, such as personal advice) being consistent with the TMD. Regulated persons distributing the product must likewise take reasonable steps for their own distribution. A distributor is not taken to fail merely because a consumer outside the target market acquires the product.
subclauses: (1) Issuer reasonable steps obligation.
(2) Not failed merely because another distributor's conduct is inconsistent, or a consumer outside the target market acquires.
(3) Distributor reasonable steps obligation.
(4) Not failed merely because a consumer outside the target market acquires.

(5) Reasonable steps are those the person is reasonably able to take, considering all relevant matters including the likelihood of inconsistent distribution and the nature and degree of harm to consumers outside the target market.
(6) Distribution necessary to implement personal advice to a particular client is not a failure of reasonable steps.
clauses.notes: Civil penalty provision. An AI distribution agent's eligibility questions, scripts, nudges and default options are part of the reasonable steps. ASIC has taken enforcement action and issued stop orders where distribution was inconsistent with TMDs. Not applicable to private health insurance products.

clauses.section_name: Part 7.8A Division 3: Distribution of financial products
clauses.heading: Record keeping and notification obligations
clauses.text: Issuers must keep complete and accurate records of TMD decisions and distribution information. Distributors must keep distribution records and report to the issuer in writing: the number of complaints received about the product within 10 business days after the end of each TMD complaints reporting period; any other information the TMD requires within 10 business days after the end of its reporting period; and any significant dealing they become aware of that is inconsistent with the TMD, as soon as practicable and in any case within 10 business days.
subclauses: (1) to (3) Record keeping by issuers and distributors.
(4) Complaints reporting to issuer within 10 business days after the end of the reporting period (ASIC Instrument 2021/784 removes the need to report nil complaints).
(5) Other TMD-specified information within 10 business days after the end of the reporting period (nil reporting relieved by Instrument 2021/784).
(6) Significant dealings inconsistent with the TMD reported to the issuer as soon as practicable and within 10 business days.
(7) to (8) Regulations and production of records to ASIC.
Offence and civil penalty for each key subsection.
clauses.notes: An AI distribution channel must log complaints and out-of-target-market sales so the distributor can meet the 10 business day reporting clocks. Not applicable to private health insurance products.

clauses.section_name: Part 7.8A Division 3: Distribution of financial products
clauses.heading: Notice to ASIC
clauses.text: An issuer that becomes aware of a significant dealing in its product that is inconsistent with the TMD (other than excluded dealings) must notify ASIC in writing as soon as practicable and in any case within 10 business days after becoming aware.
clauses.notes: Offence and civil penalty provision. Clock confirmed in the s994G text and RG 274.158. Dealings that implement personal advice are excluded. Issuers relying on AI distribution channels need aggregate monitoring to spot significant dealings early. Notifications go through the ASIC Regulatory Portal.

clauses.section_name: Part 7.10 Division 2: Market misconduct and other prohibited conduct relating to financial products and financial services
clauses.heading: Misleading or deceptive conduct (civil liability only)
clauses.text: A person must not engage in conduct in Australia, in relation to a financial product or financial service, that is misleading or deceptive or likely to mislead or deceive. Conduct in relation to a product includes dealing in, issuing, and publishing notices about it. Contravention is not an offence but gives rise to civil liability (damages under s1041I).
subclauses: (1) Prohibition on misleading or deceptive conduct in relation to financial products or services.
(2) Examples of conduct in relation to a financial product (dealing, issuing, publishing notices and others).
Not an offence; civil liability under s1041I.
clauses.notes: A breach is a deemed significant breach for breach reporting (s912D(4)(c)), so misleading AI agent output must be assessed and, where it amounts to a breach of a core obligation, reported within 30 days. Parallel to ASIC Act s12DA. Not applicable to private health insurance products.
